title: Going there, or being there?
goal: Master one rule that governs every expression of place in Icelandic: the same preposition takes two different cases, and what decides is not the place but whether there is movement.
bekal: choose þolfall for direction and þágufall for location after *í* and *á*

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Hvert ertu að fara?
dialogs.intro: Búdí runs into Sigga on the sidewalk of Laugavegur. One grammar question turns into an explanation that finally makes everything click.

lines.speaker: Sigga:
lines.text: Hæ, Búdí! Hvert ertu að fara?
lines.id: Hi, Budi! Where are you going?
lines.literal: hi, Budi! where-to are-you to go?

lines.speaker: Búdí:
lines.text: Ég er að fara í búðina. Og þú?
lines.id: I'm going to the store. And you?
lines.literal: I am to go into store-the. and you?

lines.speaker: Sigga:
lines.text: Ég er í vinnunni til fimm. Svo fer ég heim.
lines.id: I'm at work until five. Then I'm going home.
lines.literal: I am in work-the until five. then go I home.

lines.speaker: Búdí:
lines.text: Ég skil ekki. „Í búðina" en „í vinnunni"?
lines.id: I don't get it. "Í búðina" but "í vinnunni"?
lines.literal: I understand not. into store-the but in work-the?

lines.speaker: Sigga:
lines.text: Já! Þegar þú hreyfir þig: „í búðina". Þegar þú ert kyrr: „í búðinni".
lines.id: Yes! When you're moving: í búðina. When you're staying put: í búðinni.
lines.literal: yes! when you move yourself: into store-the. when you are still: in store-the.

lines.speaker: Búdí:
lines.text: Svo kemur endingin af hreyfingunni, ekki af staðnum?
lines.id: So the ending comes from the movement, not from the place?
lines.literal: so comes ending-the from movement-the, not from place-the?

lines.speaker: Sigga:
lines.text: Nákvæmlega. Ég fer á kaffihús — ég sit á kaffihúsi.
lines.id: Exactly. I go to a café — I sit at a café.
lines.literal: exactly. I go to café — I sit at café.

lines.speaker: Sigga:
lines.text: Sama hugsun. Ég fer heim, en ég er heima.
lines.id: Same idea. I go home, but I am at home.
lines.literal: same thought. I go home(ward), but I am at-home.

lines.speaker: Búdí:
lines.text: Í indónesísku segjum við líka tvö orð: „pulang" og „di rumah".
lines.id: In Indonesian we also use two words: "pulang" and "di rumah".
lines.literal: in Indonesian say we also two words: pulang and di rumah.

lines.speaker: Sigga:
lines.text: Sérðu? Þú kunnir þetta nú þegar.
lines.literal: see-you? you knew this now already.

lines.speaker: Búdí:
lines.text: Þá fer ég í búðina og svo heim. Bless!
lines.id: Then I'll go to the store and then home. Bye!
lines.literal: then go I into store-the and then home. bye!

notes: **One rule covers everything: movement calls for þolfall, staying put calls for þágufall.** *Ég fer í búð**ina*** (moving there) but *ég er í búð**inni*** (already there). Same preposition, same place; the only difference is whether anything moves.

**So don't memorize "í always takes þágufall" or anything like it** — that dead end makes many beginners give up. There is only one question to ask yourself: *does anything change place in this sentence?*

**English already gives you the mental tool.** You distinguish "to the store" from "at the store", "home" from "at home", "in" from "inside". Icelandic makes exactly the same distinction — it just marks it on the end of the noun instead of with a different preposition.
**Þegar means "when", and it changes the word order in its clause.** For now just copy the pattern; the rule comes in unit 18.

**Kunnir þetta nú þegar — "already knew this".** *Kunna* means "know how to" in the sense of having mastered a skill, unlike *geta* (be able to do something on one occasion). It's the difference between "can speak Icelandic" and "can come tomorrow".

**Sit is from sitja (sit).** Together with *standa* (stand), *liggja* (lie), and *búa* (live), it belongs to the verbs almost always followed by þágufall — because they all express **staying in a place**.

grammars.title: Í and á — one preposition, two cases
body: Compare them in pairs. The left side always involves movement; the right side always stays put.
after: Verbs that call for the left side: *fara*, *koma*, *ganga*, *hlaupa*, *keyra*, *flytja* — they all mean moving.
Verbs that call for the right side: *vera*, *búa*, *sitja*, *standa*, *vinna*, *bíða* — they all mean being somewhere.

⚠️ The same rule applies to *yfir* (over), *undir* (under), *fyrir* (in front of), and *við* (beside). Four more prepositions, one rule — so once you've mastered it for *í* and *á*, you've mastered it for all of them.

grammars.title: Adverb pairs: direction and location
body: Icelandic has two separate words where English often gets by with one. The form ending in **-a** always means staying put.
after: Now the three question words promised in unit 2 are complete: **hvert** where to, **hvar** where, **hvaðan** where from. English once had the same trio — *whither*, *where*, *whence*; Icelandic still uses all three every day.
*Heim* and *heima* are the pair you'll hear most. *Ég fer heim* — I'm going home. *Ég er heima* — I'm at home. *Ég er heiman* — I'm away from home, a rare third form, but it exists.

sections.title: Í or á? — a choice to memorize

blocks.text: The case rule is clear, but the choice between *í* and *á* doesn't always have a reason. Most of it can be guessed: *í* for places with walls and a roof, *á* for surfaces and open places. The rest has to be memorized.

blocks.title: Á Íslandi — one preposition that marks a nation
items: Countries usually take *í*: *í Noregi*, *í Danmörku*, *í Indónesíu*. But Iceland itself takes **á**: *á Íslandi*, *til Íslands*, *frá Íslandi*.

The reason is simple: Iceland is an **island**, and islands take *á* — just like *á Grænlandi*, *á Sikiley*. *Í Íslandi* sounds wrong to Icelandic ears straight away, so learn this one as a single chunk.
The same habit applies to towns within the country: *í Reykjavík* (in a valley), but *á Akureyri* (on a shore). If you're not sure, ask — Icelanders actually enjoy being asked about this.

blocks.text: *Flugvöllur* is literally "flight field" and *sjúkrahús* "sick house" — word for word, just like English *airfield*. Take apart every compound you meet; half your new vocabulary will come free that way.

exercises.prompt: Choose the right form: direction or location.
items: Ég kem í ____ (vinnuna, vinnunni) klukkan átta.
